strengths: Well-motivated conceptual contribution addressing the semantic-kinematic gap in VLA models; the argument that reasoning should occur in action space rather than vision-language space is clearly articulated and intuitive
Strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks with particularly notable +8.4% improvement on LIBERO-Plus robustness benchmark, demonstrating practical value for distribution shift robustness
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablation studies (Tables 4-6), analysis of design choices, real-world deployment, and cross-embodiment transfer
Methodologically sound architecture with well-motivated EAR and IAR designs that are complementary; efficient downsampling strategy in IAR addresses computational concerns
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendices, and public benchmark evaluations enabling verification of results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: both EAR and IAR employ standard transformer components; self-conditioning in generative models is established, with novelty primarily in application rather than methodology

Insufficient analysis of core claims: paper lacks visualization, interpretation, or mechanistic explanation of why action-space reasoning works better; no evidence that modules learn 'kinematically coherent' representations

Methodological concern with teacher forcing stabilization (Section 3.4): using ground-truth reference trajectories during training introduces privileged information; train-test mismatch at inference is not analyzed

Baseline dependency makes isolated contribution unclear: improvements over π0.5 are incremental; individual module gains are modest (1.4% for EAR, 1.2% for IAR), suggesting cumulative rather than individual benefit
Weak contribution from Implicit Action Reasoner: IAR provides only ~1.2% gain on LIBERO; marginal differences across three KV-cache strategies (~0.3%) suggest limited necessity of this component
Limited real-world evaluation: only 3 tasks on primary platform; absolute success rates modest (~66.7%); cross-embodiment transfer shown for only one task; comparisons limited to π0 and π0.5
Computational overhead is non-trivial: 23% latency increase (91ms→112ms) and 0.46B parameter increase may limit deployment on real-time systems; claims of 'marginal' overhead are debatable
Scattered hyperparameter sensitivity results (Table 5) provide unclear design principles; many hyperparameters introduced with limited systematic sensitivity analysis

Missing comparative analysis of reasoning modalities: no ablation directly comparing action space vs. language space vs. vision space; most relevant baseline (CoT-VLA visual reasoning) not discussed in depth
Generalization questions unaddressed: modest improvements on LIBERO (1.6%) and VLABench (+3.3% IS); unclear which task characteristics benefit from action-space reasoning; no task-dependent analysis

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying the semantic-kinematic gap in existing VLA models, providing principled rationale for action-space reasoning
Extensive experimental coverage across multiple simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench) with thorough ablation studies systematically decomposing EAR and IAR contributions
Strong improvements on LIBERO-Plus (+8.4% over π0.5), suggesting better generalization under distribution shift, which is practically important
Real-world deployment on multiple robotic platforms (AgiBot G1, AgileX) demonstrates commitment to practical validation
Technically sound architectural design with reasonable component choices (transformer-based EAR, cross-attention IAR, dual-head fusion)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution of action-space intermediate supervision is not fundamentally new—self-conditioning in generative models and action priors in imitation learning are well-established. Distinction is primarily application/framing, not conceptual innovation.

Marginal improvements on primary LIBERO benchmark (only 1.6% absolute gain: 98.5% vs 96.9%) without statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals—results may be within noise margin given benchmark saturation around 98-99%

Significant train-test mismatch: During training, Zex computed from ground-truth trajectories (teacher forcing), but at inference from EAR predictions (self-conditioning). No ablation justifies this choice or analyzes its impact on actual learning

Insufficient analysis of what model learns: No visualizations of reference trajectories, no analysis of implicit priors, no failure case studies, and critically—no investigation of why approach helps LIBERO-Plus much more than LIBERO
Limited real-world validation: Only 3 tasks with small trial counts (24, 60, 40 trials); success rates substantially lower than simulation (66.7% vs 98.5%); no real-world comparisons to other methods

Questionable design choices appear ad-hoc: Reference horizon (Href=15) ≠ output horizon (H=10) with unclear justification; M=1 for IAR queries severely constrains mechanism; d'=128 downsampling dimension arbitrary; loss weights λ1=λ2=0.5 unjustified

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: 23% latency increase (91ms→112ms) and 3.3B→3.8B parameters—while paper acknowledges deployment concerns as 'limitation,' this deserves serious discussion for robot deployment claims
Weaker results on VLABench (47.4% overall, smaller improvement over baseline) suggests approach is less beneficial on diverse/complex tasks; paper does not investigate why

Missing experimental rigor: No significance testing, confidence intervals, or sensitivity analyses; some baselines reproduced 'by us' introducing potential variance; unclear if all methods use identical training setup
Reproducibility concerns: Code not released (or not mentioned); depends on π0.5 which may not be public; details missing on reference trajectory construction; no ablation on teacher forcing strategy

strengths: Compelling conceptual contribution: The semantic-kinematic gap identification and action-space reasoning paradigm is well-motivated and represents meaningful conceptual progress in VLA research

Comprehensive experimental validation: Strong results across three diverse simulation benchmarks (98.5% LIBERO, 84.1% LIBERO-Plus, 47.4% VLABench) with particularly impressive robustness gains under distribution shifts (+11.6% camera, +16.3% robot state)
Well-designed complementary architecture: EAR and IAR components show strong synergy with ablations clearly demonstrating individual (+1.4%, +1.2%) and combined (+1.6%) contributions
Excellent reproducibility and transparency: Comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and honest discussion of limitations in well-organized appendices
Real-world validation across multiple platforms: Demonstration on both AgiBot G1 and AgileX shows cross-embodiment adaptability, moving beyond simulation-only evaluation
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with effective motivation (Figure 1) and architecture visualization (Figure 2)
weaknesses: Fair comparison concerns: Unexplained baseline discrepancies (π0.5 reported as 98.8% in original work vs 96.9% in Table 1); many improvements are 1-2 percentage points without statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error analysis

Training-test mismatch via teacher forcing: Z^ex computed from ground-truth trajectories during training but predicted trajectories during inference—this distribution shift is significant but only briefly mentioned, potentially limiting EAR effectiveness at test time

Limited technical novelty: Individual components use standard architectures (transformers with cross-attention); primary contribution is conceptual framing and combination rather than architectural innovation

Insufficient analysis of learned representations: No visualizations of EAR-generated reference trajectories or IAR-extracted action priors; lacking qualitative evidence for why action-space reasoning works better

Non-monotonic scaling with EAR parameters: Table 10 shows performance drops when EAR exceeds 300M parameters, suggesting method requires careful tuning; explanation is speculative and raises questions about robustness

Limited real-world validation: Only 3 tasks across small sample sizes (24-40 trials per condition) with more modest improvements (5.7% vs 1.6% on simulation); real-world results lack statistical analysis
Computational overhead not fully addressed: 23% latency increase (91→112ms) and 460M additional parameters may be problematic for resource-constrained platforms; cost-benefit analysis insufficient
Identified but unaddressed fundamental limitation: Paper acknowledges action representation as 'chunks' lacks geometric structure that could limit ACoT potential, yet doesn't address this

Incomplete analysis of when ACoT helps: While showing best results on long-horizon tasks (+3.6% LIBERO-Long), lacks systematic analysis of which task properties benefit most or guidance for practitioners on applicability
VLABench results less impressive: 47.4% performance with only incremental improvements over baselines (43.1%→47.4%), suggesting potential dataset/task dependence

strengths: Well-motivated conceptual contribution: The semantic-kinematic gap argument and action-space reasoning paradigm represent a genuine and clearly articulated perspective distinct from prior language-based and vision-based CoT approaches.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench) and real-world robots, with systematic ablations, sim-to-real transfer evaluation, and extensive supplementary analysis.
Strong and consistent empirical improvements, particularly on distribution-shifted data (LIBERO-Plus +8.4%) and real-world tasks, demonstrating practical applicability and generalization benefits.

Thorough experimental methodology following official protocols with detailed implementation details, reproducibility support, and fair baseline comparisons; extensive ablation studies provide valuable insights into design choices.
Clear presentation with effective motivation, well-structured writing, and figures that clearly illustrate conceptual differences from prior work; detailed appendices support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: EAR and IAR employ standard transformers and cross-attention mechanisms; flow-matching is borrowed from existing generative model self-conditioning; architecture primarily combines existing techniques with minimal algorithmic innovation.

Training-inference mismatch inadequately addressed: During training, reference trajectories are computed from ground-truth (teacher forcing), preventing the model from learning to predict good references. Inference switches to self-conditioned mode, creating distribution shift. This critical design choice lacks rigorous analysis of its impact on downstream reasoning quality.

Modest improvements on standard benchmarks: 1.6% absolute gain on LIBERO (98.5% vs 96.9%) does not strongly justify 23% latency increase (91ms→112ms) and 14% parameter growth (3.35B→3.81B), particularly for resource-constrained robotic deployment where real-time constraints are critical.

Insufficient analysis of implicit action priors: Claims that VLM internal representations encode useful action distributions lack empirical validation. No visualization, interpretability analysis, or theoretical justification for why these latent features should capture action-relevant information. Table 6's finding that downsampling works best raises unanswered questions about what information is actually useful.

Statistical rigor concerns: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported. Real-world experiments use small sample sizes (24-40 trials per task). No multiple runs or cross-validation. Unclear whether reported improvements are statistically significant versus noise.

strengths: Well-motivated core insight about the semantic-kinematic gap and benefits of action-space reasoning over language/visual intermediates
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench) with extensive ablations and real-world validation on multiple robot platforms
Consistent performance improvements across diverse settings, with particularly strong robustness gains on distribution-shifted LIBERO-Plus zero-shot transfer
Practical real-world deployment demonstrating applicability beyond simulation with cross-embodiment validation
Clear presentation of the core motivation through effective visualizations and problem formulation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: EAR and IAR are standard transformer components (cross-attention to VLM cache, learnable queries with pooling); the core contribution reduces to reference trajectory conditioning, which is incremental rather than fundamentally novel

Critical methodological concern: Teacher forcing during training (using ground-truth Z^ex) versus inference (using predicted Z^ex from π^ref) creates train-test mismatch that is acknowledged but not adequately addressed or quantified
Modest empirical improvements on saturated benchmarks (+1.6% on LIBERO, +3.3% on VLABench IS) that may be partly attributed to additional parameters/compute rather than conceptual innovation

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: No visualization or analysis of learned representations (Z^ex, Z^im); unclear what action-relevant information IAR actually extracts versus generic VLM features

Hyperparameter sensitivity and non-monotonic scaling: EAR performance is non-monotonic with parameter count (Table 10), suggesting brittleness; balance factors λ₁, λ₂ and reference horizon choices lack principled justification or sensitivity analysis

Overstated conceptual distinction from prior work: All three CoT paradigms (language, vision, action) are intermediate supervision signals; the claim that action-space conditioning is fundamentally superior lacks rigorous validation
Limited real-world scope: Only 3 tasks with 24-40 trials each; cross-embodiment validation on single additional platform; all tasks are tabletop manipulation
Incomplete reproducibility: GitHub link provided is incomplete; code not yet available; hyperparameter choices (M=1, d'=128) lack justification
